newsitem.title: UK: Silver moves East but prices fail to respond - CRU.
newsitem.headline: Silver moves East but prices fail to respond - CRU.

text.p: Large tonnages of silver have been moved from the United States, Britain and Switzerland apparently to the Middle and Far East during the first seven months of this year, according to CRU International's Precious Metals Monitor.
Even so the price was under pressure, reaching an 18-month low fix of $4.8475 on September 29 and again on October 1.
"While rising demand should help (silver) claw its way back above $5.00 in coming weeks, further significant gains are unlikely," the CRU report said.
The most recent stock figures from Comex for October 7 show stocks fell 1,149,955 ounces to 139,493,089 ounces.

The stock declines have been accompanied by rising US bullion exports but unlike last year when the same pattern occurred, lease rates in London and New York are too similar to make arbitrage deals profitable.
"Instead, substantial US exports appear to be part of a convoluted tripping exercise via Europe to the East," according the CRU report.
Data for the first seven months of the year show US exports totalled 1,900 tonnes, more than twice the level exported in the same period last year.
US exports to the UK totalled 1,036 tonnes 240 percent higher than in the 1995 period and exports to Switzerland totalled 170 tonnes by the end of July.
The European exports appear to be re-routed eastwards. Of the UK's 1,166 tonnes of total silver exports in the first seven months, 1,040 were exported.
Swiss exports during the same period totalled 1,477 tonnes exceeding imports of 1,285 tonnes.
UK customs data show exports to the United Arab Emirates, Singapore and India totalled 767 tonnes in the first seven months of the year, over double the 1995 level.
Re-exports to Dubai were 8.4 percent ahead up to August at 586 tonnes and "these too confirm a picture of strengthening demand in the Far East", according to CRU.
However, despite apparently buoyant demand, Indian silver prices have slipped with the London fixing.
"Silver stocks are still proving sufficiently large to negate the impact of the sizeable cumulative (supply-demand) deficit which has accrued," the report said.
Whether or not the draw on stocks will be sufficient to boost prices is still unclear.
According to the World Silver Institute's World Silver Production Forecast, by 1999 western world mine output should increase to 14,420 tonnes from 12,184 tonnes in 1995.
"If such an increase is achieved it would go a substantial way towards bringing the market more closely into balance, threatening future price rises," CRU said.
CRU's analysis of silver production for the first nine months of this year suggested an uptrend has already begun.
Led by Canada and Peru, mine output increase by three percent during the period to 8,830 tonnes.
